newsitem.title: GERMANY: Prosecutors probe last Bremer Vulkan CEO.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutors probe last Bremer Vulkan CEO.

text.p: German prosecutors said on Monday they had launched a probe against two former executives of bankrupt shipyard group Bremer Vulkan Verbund AG, which collapsed under a mountain of debt just over a year ago.

Horst Nullmeyer, a prosecutor for the city-state of Bremen, said he was investigating former chief executive Udo Wagner over a contractual clause which guaranteed a 10 million mark severance payment if Bremer Vulkan went bankrupt.
Nullmeyer told Reuters the money had been transferred to a trust account and later withdrawn.
He added he was also investigating supervisory board chairman Hero Brahms, who would have been responsible for signing such a deal with Wagner.
Neither of the two former Bremer executives could be reached for comment immediately.

Bremer Vulkan declared bankruptcy in May 1996 after posting huge losses and is under investigation over allegedly misappropriating 850 million marks of state aid cleared by the European Union for use in eastern Germany.

The Bremen city parliament's committee investigating the Vulkan affair 10 days ago heard details of an agreement with the company's banks guaranteeing Wagner an income of six million marks over three years, whether or not the company failed.

Wagner, who will testify before the committee this Friday, started working at Vulkan on February 1, 1996. The company became insolvent three weeks later, and Wagner left Vulkan when bankruptcy proceedings opened on the following May 1.

Separately, Germany's BAWe stock market watchdog recently launched an insider trading investigation after Bremer Vulkan shares spiked in April on takeover speculation. The company's stock has since fallen back to trade at 5.70 marks on Monday, down from a pre-collapse price of over 80 marks.
